vignette:
Layla was 38, a divorced Middle Eastern woman who had built a life around structure and responsibility as a school principal, but after the combat event that disrupted it, even the most ordinary settings began to feel altered. She had been near the violence in a way she still struggled to explain in a clean sequence. When she tried to tell the story, the pieces did not stay in order. She knew there had been sounds before she understood what was happening, and later movement, confusion, and the urgent sense that there was nowhere safe to stand still. When she described it, she would stop and start again, frustrated that she could not put the moments in the right order. What stayed with her most were fragments that came back with unnerving force: a sound she had heard during the frightening event would suddenly appear in her mind, as if it were happening again inside her head. At those moments, she became tense and irritable, her jaw tightening as if she were still bracing for impact. When the memory came, it was not only fear that rose in her; she also felt a hot, intense rage that startled her because it felt so immediate, so unsorted, and so unlike the composed authority she showed at work.

In the months afterward, Layla found that she was on guard even inside her own home. She checked the locks more than once, listened for noises in the hallway, and found herself identifying ways out of rooms without meaning to. Before she could relax anywhere, she automatically noticed doors, windows, stairwells, and the nearest route to leave. This habit followed her into the school building as well, where she would glance toward exits during meetings and position herself so she could see the main doorway. In her apartment, she said she felt unable to fully settle, as if the walls themselves could not be counted on to keep her safe. The vigilance was accompanied by strong negative emotions that arrived without much warning: fear when a noise sounded too sudden, horror when an image flashed into her mind, anger that could flare when she heard news reports, and guilt and shame that she did not fully know how to name. She was troubled by how exposed she felt to these reactions, especially because she had spent years being the person others relied on.

As the weeks turned into months, Layla's view of other people changed. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, and this belief showed up in everyday interactions as carefully held distance. She was civil at school, but less open, more guarded in conversations with colleagues and parents. She no longer assumed that anyone's reassurance would hold. The divorce that had already separated her from her former life felt, in her mind, like another confirmation that she could not depend on others to stay steady when things became difficult. Even in friendships, she watched for signs that someone might disappoint her or fail to understand. What she had once taken for normal human reliability now seemed fragile, and she kept herself emotionally back from it.

Layla also spoke with painful self-criticism about how she had handled life since the event. She was certain that her reactions showed she was a lousy coper. She compared herself unfavorably to the competent, organized principal she used to be, and the contrast left her ashamed. She noticed how little meaning she could attach to the routines that had once mattered to her. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore, she said, even the work she had poured herself into. At school, she still carried out the demands of the role, but the purpose behind it felt muted, as if she were moving through obligations rather than toward something she believed in. That loss was not abstract; it showed up in the way she got through each day, doing what needed to be done while feeling detached from the sense that it added up to anything.

By the time she sought help, Layla was exhausted by how much effort it took to remain outwardly functional while inwardly unsettled. She came in after noticing that the constant scanning, the sudden waves of fear and anger, and the intrusive sounds in her mind were crowding into both her home life and her work. What finally pushed her to ask for treatment was the worry that she could not keep carrying all of this alone without becoming even more isolated. She was not sure she expected trust to come easily again, but she hoped that speaking about the event in a way that made sense of its broken sequence might help her feel less trapped inside it. More than anything, she wanted to feel safe enough at home to stop looking for exits in every room.
